title: Develop, implement and manage a permaculture site design

lessons.title: Permaculture ethics, principles and site analysis
lessons.html:
What is permaculture?

Permaculture is a design approach for productive, self-sustaining land-use systems modelled on natural ecosystems. It is used on smallholdings, community gardens, school food gardens and rural homesteads across South Africa, and its ideas can be applied on commercial farms too.

The three ethics

  • Earth care: look after soil, water, plants and animals.
  • People care: meet people's needs for food, shelter and community.
  • Fair share: limit consumption and return surplus to the system and community.

Key design principles

  • Observe and interact before acting.
  • Catch and store energy and water.
  • Each element performs several functions, and each function is supported by several elements.
  • Use and value diversity and edges.
  • Use small, slow solutions and learn from feedback.
  • Produce no waste: outputs of one element are inputs to another.

Site analysis

Spend time observing before designing, ideally through different seasons.

FactorWhat to record
ClimateRainfall season and amount, frost, prevailing and hot winds
SunSun path in summer and winter, shade from buildings and trees
WaterWhere runoff flows, where it ponds, existing sources
Slope and soilContours, soil depth, texture, drainage
VegetationExisting useful plants, invasive aliens
People and accessPaths, needs of users, security

Draw a base map showing boundaries, buildings, water, slopes and sectors (directions from which sun, wind, fire and noise come).

lessons.title: Designing zones, water and soil systems
lessons.html:
Putting the design together

Zones

Zones place elements according to how often they need attention.

  • Zone 0: the home.
  • Zone 1: closest; herbs, salad vegetables, seedlings, worm farm, daily visits.
  • Zone 2: fruit trees, larger vegetable beds, chickens, compost.
  • Zone 3: field crops, orchards, grazing.
  • Zone 4: managed woodland, foraging, firewood.
  • Zone 5: wild area left for nature and observation.

Sectors

Use sector analysis to place windbreaks against cold or hot dry winds, firebreaks on the fire-risk side, and to make use of winter sun on the north side (in the southern hemisphere).

Water harvesting

  • Collect roof water in tanks.
  • Build swales (level trenches on contour with a mound below) to slow, spread and sink runoff into the soil, planting trees on the mound.
  • Use mulched basins around trees, and greywater from washing for fruit trees where it is safe and lawful.
  • Small ponds can support irrigation and wildlife; fence them for child safety.

Building soil

  • Compost and worm farming to recycle kitchen and garden waste.
  • Thick mulch to protect soil, hold moisture and feed soil life.
  • No-dig or trench beds.
  • Legumes and green manures to add nitrogen.

Plant guilds and food forests

A guild is a group of plants supporting each other, for example a fruit tree with nitrogen-fixing plants, pest-repelling herbs, ground covers and deep-rooted plants that mine nutrients. Food forests stack layers: canopy, small trees, shrubs, herbs, ground cover, climbers and roots. Choose species adapted to the local climate, including indigenous plants, and avoid invasive species listed under South African regulations.

lessons.title: Implementing and managing the design
lessons.html:
From paper to practice

Implementation plan

  1. Priorities: start with water harvesting and soil building, then zones 1 and 2.
  2. Phasing: break work into stages matched to season, labour and budget. Plant trees at the start of the rainy season.
  3. Resources: list materials (mulch, manure, tanks, seed, trees), labour and tools; source locally and reuse materials.
  4. Budget in ZAR and identify income streams such as vegetable sales, seedlings, eggs, workshops.
  5. People: involve users or the community in design and work so they own and maintain it.

Animals in the design

Chickens can work as pest control, weeders and manure producers in rotated runs or chicken tractors. Ducks help with snails. Manage animals humanely under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 with shelter, water and protection from predators.

Ongoing management

  • Observe regularly: pests, plant health, water flow after rain, soil moisture.
  • Keep a garden diary: planting dates, yields, problems and solutions.
  • Rotate annual beds; save seed from strong, adapted plants.
  • Manage pests with diversity, companion plants, hand picking, traps and encouraging birds and beneficial insects.
  • Adjust the design as you learn.

Evaluating success

Measure food produced, water used, money saved or earned, soil improvement (organic matter, earthworms), biodiversity and how well users' needs are met. Compare with your goals.

Safety

Use tools safely, lift correctly, wear gloves when handling manure and compost, cover tanks and ponds to keep children safe, and keep any chemicals locked away.

Key points

  • Permaculture rests on earth care, people care and fair share.
  • Observe the site thoroughly before designing.
  • Use zones and sectors to place elements efficiently.
  • Harvest water and build soil first.
  • Implement in phases, involve users and keep observing and adjusting.
